# This week in AI-native companies

### Buzz, OpenWorker, the files convergence, 12-factor companies — and the question none of them answer.

A short Friday digest for people building companies with AI in the middle of them: what shipped, what got funded, and what it means, from a founder running his company this way. First edition, so it reaches back a little further than a week.

Signal of the week: Block launched Buzz. Jack Dorsey’s team shipped a free, open-source workspace where humans and AI agents share channels, and the agents are members, not bots: their own identity, their own keys, signing their own work ( Block’s announcement , TechCrunch ). About 6,700 GitHub stars in its first two days. The launch discourse’s own top question, raised by a Slack employee no less: once agent teammates can see everything, who decides what each one should see? Identity, it turns out, was the easy half.

Andrew Ng launched OpenWorker, and YC asked for the team version. OpenWorker (built with Rohit Prasad, ex-Alexa) is an open-source, local-first personal agent that “delivers finished work, not just chat,” runs on your machine with any model, and checks in before doing anything consequential. The same week, Y Combinator’s new Requests for Startups asked for “Multiplayer AI”: shared agent sessions a team can watch, redirect, and hand off. Between Buzz, OpenWorker, and YC’s ask, the agent-as-coworker got named from three directions in seven days.

Everyone is converging on plain files. LangChain’s OpenWiki Brains , Vault-LD 0.5 , and Google’s Open Knowledge Format: three independent moves formalizing markdown as agent memory within days of each other ( The New Stack’s read : the moat is shifting from the model to the markdown a team owns). Files won because humans and agents can both read them. The unglamorous part nobody’s product does for you: keeping the files true.

Chroma’s CEO proposed “12-factor companies.” Jeff Huber, in the lineage of 12-factor apps: own your context, rent your intelligence, develop rubrics, encode your expertise. The standout line: “The old firm bundled labor and coordination. The new firm bundles context and authority.”
